title: The Trouble with Food Miles
subtitle: Why the distance food travels says surprisingly little about its effect on the climate

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In the early years of this century, the idea of 'food miles' became one of the most successful slogans of the environmental movement. The reasoning seemed straightforward: food transported over long distances burns more fuel, so eating food grown close to home must be better for the planet. Several supermarkets began labelling products that had been flown in from abroad, and some campaigners proposed that every item should carry a figure showing how far it had travelled. The concept had the great advantage of being easy to understand and easy to act upon. It also appealed to a widespread unease about globalised supply chains and to a feeling that food from familiar places must be more trustworthy. Its weakness, as researchers soon began to point out, was that it measured the wrong thing.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The most comprehensive analysis to date, published in 2018, combined data from roughly 38,000 farms in 119 countries to estimate the greenhouse gas emissions associated with different foods across their whole life cycle, from the clearing of land to the supermarket shelf. Transport, it found, accounted on average for less than a tenth of the total. For most foods, by far the largest share of emissions arises on the farm itself: from fertiliser, from the methane produced by cattle and sheep as they digest grass, and from the clearing of forests to create pasture and cropland. Beef produced with the lowest emissions, the study concluded, still generated many times more greenhouse gases than the most carbon-intensive peas or beans.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Distance can even mislead. A frequently cited study from New Zealand compared lamb raised there and shipped to Britain with lamb raised in Britain itself, and concluded that the imported meat had the lower carbon footprint, because New Zealand's sheep graze outdoors all year round on grass that grows with little fertiliser, while British farms rely more heavily on supplementary feed. In the same way, tomatoes grown in heated greenhouses in northern Europe during the winter may be responsible for more emissions than tomatoes grown outdoors in Spain and carried north by lorry. Critics of the New Zealand study noted that it had been produced by researchers in an exporting country, and that its results depended on assumptions about British farming that not everyone accepted. Yet even sceptics acknowledged that its basic point, that where and how food is produced matters more than how far it travels, was sound.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: There is one important exception. Food carried by air produces far more emissions per kilogram than food carried by ship, often fifty times as much or more. Fresh fish, asparagus, green beans and soft fruit such as berries, flown out of season from distant countries can therefore have a substantial transport footprint. But air freight carries only a tiny proportion of the world's food, and the products concerned are usually easy to identify, since they tend to be perishable goods on sale outside their normal season. A simpler rule, to be wary of food that has been flown, would capture most of what is valuable in the food-miles idea without its distortions, although, as will become clear, even this rule has complications.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Supporters of local food do not rest their case on carbon alone, and it would be unfair to suggest that they do. Buying from nearby farms, they argue, keeps money within the community, helps to preserve farmland and traditional varieties, and reconnects consumers with the seasons and with the people who grow what they eat. Dr Hannah Okoro, a rural sociologist who has studied farmers' markets in England, found that customers valued the conversations they had with producers almost as much as the produce itself. These are legitimate considerations, and nothing in the evidence on emissions undermines them. A thriving local food economy may also make a region less vulnerable to disruptions in international trade, as the shortages of the pandemic years reminded many people. The difficulty arises only when they are presented as environmental benefits that they do not, in fact, deliver.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Some economists go further and argue that the emphasis on local food may harm people in poorer countries. Professor Daniel Mwangi, who studies agricultural trade, points out that tens of thousands of smallholders in East Africa depend on exports of vegetables and flowers to Europe. Kenyan beans grown with little machinery or artificial fertiliser and flown to Britain may, he suggests, generate fewer emissions in total than some beans grown in heated conditions in Europe, despite the flight. Admittedly, such comparisons are contested, and the figures depend heavily on the assumptions used. But a campaign that persuaded European shoppers to boycott air-freighted produce would fall hardest on some of the world's poorest farmers, for an environmental gain that is far from certain.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this means that the distance food travels is irrelevant; it means that distance is a poor guide to what matters most. For consumers who want to reduce the environmental impact of their diet, the evidence points overwhelmingly in one direction: what we eat matters far more than where it comes from. Replacing a portion of beef with beans, wherever each was grown, does more for the climate than any amount of careful attention to labels showing distance. Food miles succeeded because they offered a simple measure for a complicated problem. The lesson of their failure is not that simple measures are useless, but that a measure is only as good as its connection to the thing it is meant to represent.
